summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Palau. The Penal Code signed by President Tommy Remengesau Jr. in April 2014 took effect on 23 July 2014 and contains no offence outlawing consensual sex between people of the same sex. It repealed the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment. Before that repeal, male same-sex sexual activity was an offence while female same-sex activity was not. Palau's Attorney General confirmed the change to the Human Dignity Trust.

Palau has no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ residents do not hold the same legal protections as non-LGBTQ residents. No protective provision specific to gender identity appears in the available material.

The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman. The same-sex marriage ban was one of 22 amendments approved in the referendum of 4 November 2008, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read under Palauan law as same-sex therefore has no route to marriage or to those protections. In July 2019 President Remengesau Jr. said he supported striking down the constitutional ban as discriminatory and believed in full equality; no repeal outcome is recorded.

Palau provides no legal gender recognition. No provision for updating identity documents, no screening or facility rules, no custody rule and no gender-affirming care provision specific to transgender people is recorded in the available material, and no transgender-specific penalty or enforcement measure exists.

At its 2011 Universal Periodic Review Palau accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts and to combat discrimination, and in October 2011 the government promised to fully decriminalise homosexuality. On 22 March 2011 Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint Human Rights Council statement calling for an end to violence, criminal sanctions and related human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Palau's 2014 decriminalisation was reported alongside São Tomé, and the global count of countries retaining anti-sodomy offences fell to 79 as a result (Erasing 76crimes, 16 October 2014). The figure is a count of jurisdictions, not a measure of relative risk.

As of around 2011 Palau appeared among more than 70 Pacific and global jurisdictions whose laws still criminalised same-sex relations. That snapshot predates the Penal Code in force since 23 July 2014 and no longer describes Palauan law.

The joint statement of 22 March 2011 is a political declaration delivered on behalf of 84 countries; it carries no binding force and establishes no enforcement mechanism in Palau.

Presidential support for repeal of the constitutional marriage ban, expressed in July 2019, is a statement of position by the head of state rather than a legal change, and no legislative or judicial outcome follows from it in the available material.
localsOnly:

No anti-discrimination statute in Palau covers sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no statutory basis for complaints on those grounds.

No legal gender recognition procedure is provided for residents, and the available material records no route to amending gender markers on identity documents.

The Attorney General's confirmation of the 2014 repeal and the government's October 2011 decriminalisation commitment are the documented official positions; the July 2019 presidential statement on the marriage ban has no recorded outcome.
outOfScopeNotes:
The available material contains no information on violence against transgender people in Palau, no incident records, no killing figures and no general homicide rate against which any such figure could be compared. Nothing in the inventory documents patterned or state-tolerated targeting.

Entry and visa rules, border or airport screening practice, document-marker rules, facility access, custody outcomes and access to gender-affirming care are not sourced for Palau, and no claim about them can be made from this inventory.

Whether the July 2019 presidential statement in favour of striking down the constitutional ban produced a subsequent amendment, bill or court ruling is unresolved in the available material.

Whether any administrative route to legal gender recognition exists outside the cited sources, for example under the 2014 Penal Code or subordinate regulation, is not sourced.
